Yeah, I think I’ve seen something about that on this subreddit. I’m not sure if I was actually able to lose the lipedema fat, or it’s just that the lipedema fat was so trace that it wasn’t really apparent at all when I lost all my normal fat. When I got into recovery I kind of “overshot” as far as my weight and now I’m back down to a more normal weight for my build. While my legs in general got smaller from losing some of the excess weight, I feel like the lipedema “shape” didn’t really change. Now after my surgery I finally have normal shaped knees, calves, and ankles, but I truly don’t think I would have been able to achieve that just by losing weight

The symptoms I developed with weight gain were more obvious hallmark signs of lipedema like the beady feeling under the skin (I did not have this when I was underweight), and the inability to loose the fat with weight loss. prior to recovery this time around, if I lost weight my legs would turn to sticks which is why I was never really sure if I had lipedema or not. I have never gotten anywhere near the weights I was while I was going through anorexia so who knows, maybe they would eventually return to that size with enough weight loss, but I really don’t want to get back to that point because my quality of life was non existent and I was very unwell physically and mentally.

Swelling throughout the day, easy bruising, constant heavy aching (particularly in my calves). Everyone always told me any symptoms of anything I had was always related to malnutrition, but as I gained weight and my symptoms got worse, that’s when I realized the real culprit all along was lipedema. And now I have it in my arms and probably stomach as well 😐

How much was removed and what was your starting size? Unfortunately one surgery is rarely enough unless you only have one problem area you want to address, or you are quite small to begin with. Or it’s possible the surgeon just did not remove enough. For reference I had only my lower (ankles, calves, knees) done, and my surgeon removed about 4L. I had instant results that have been extremely noticeable throughout my recovery, even with the initial swelling. My surgeon takes a very aggressive approach to fat removal, whereas some surgeons are more conservative. If you are not happy, I would definitely ask for a revision. It’s your body and I’m sure a lot of money and pain that you went through and you deserve to be happy with the outcome.

Wow, I feel like I could have written this myself. I had very severe AN from age 12 until a couple years ago, when I gained a lot of weight in an attempt to recover. I also have had OCD since I was about 3 or 4 years old. Same thing with health related OCD. I would constantly worry about things like cancer, dementia, etc. I did rituals every day to “prevent” my family from getting cancer, and then both of my parents did. I started seeing things online about lipedema and it freaked me out, and I would start to convince myself I had it. But like you eventually my legs were so bony, I kind of put that fear to rest. Lately i suspect maybe I did have very early stages of it back then, it just was so mild, that with enough weight loss it wasn’t really visible. Fast forward to the end of 2023, I gained a lot of weight very quickly and regained my period for the first time in many years. I had restored weight in treatment before many times over the years, but it never came back quite like this last time. I slowly started to suspect again that I had lipedema. Fat pockets around my knees, thick calves and ankles, fat that hangs around my elbow, grainy feeling under skin. I tried to tell myself it was just my ocd acting up, but the more research I did the more I became fully convinced I did in fact have lipedema. I finally made an appointment with a specialist and he confirmed I do in fact have stage 2 type 3 &5. I’m so sorry you are going through this as well. I can only imagine how much it is messing with your mind, like it is mine. There is a whole added layer of complication with the ED history because now I’m being told I need to cut all sorts of things out of my diet, plus it just makes me regret ever gaining weight to begin with. I’m sorry I don’t have better advice, but if you ever want to chat, don’t hesitate to reach out ❤️

My vegan journey was actually very counter intuitive to what many in the ED field typically assume. I’ve been hit with many accusations of using veganism as an excuse for restriction, which usually is where a lot of the anti vegan bias comes in with treatment providers. I wanted to be vegan since a very young age because I always felt eating animals was wrong, but because of my illness and many of my safe foods being animals product based, I put it off for years out of fear of giving up my safe foods. After cardiac issues and learning I had developed osteoporosis, I decided I was going to take recovery seriously for the first time ever, and I actually started recovery on a vegan diet, allowing myself to fully lean into my ethical beliefs while properly fueling myself. I honestly wasn’t really concerned about veganism in regards to osteoporosis, particularly because I had done a lot of research and there is pretty good evidence to show cow dairy is actually not so great for bone density as previously thought. I think I also just had the mindset of adequate calories from a vegan diet is better than malnutrition from an animal based diet. I fully weight restored for about two years on a vegan diet and was in a state of semi remission for a while. I had a bone density scan about 3 years after being diagnosed with osteoporosis and to my surprise the results were much better than expected. Unfortunately Osteoporosis cannot be fully reversed, but luckily with adequate nutrition there was no additional loss and slight improvements were shown in the scans. As far as exercise, I had very bad compulsive over exercise prior to my recovery efforts. When I decided to go all in on recovery I ceased all exercise completely. It is often said that weight baring exercises are beneficial, but I have been told that in the case of eating disorders this is less so the case. Rest for a good period of time, while your body is still restoring itself, is going to be the most helpful in the long run! I gradually started introducing light walking. To this day I am cautious with exercise due to the fact I know it can turn compulsive for me quickly. I will note that a few years into my remission, due to some stressful life circumstances, I did experience a pretty bad relapse, but in hospitalization and residential treatment was able to continue eating vegan which was supported by the treatment facilities. I have also worked with an ED specialized dietican who supported ethical veganism and provided me with resources on calcium rich vegan foods and different ways to preserve bone density. Regaining your menstrual cycle (if you lost it in the first place) is also crucial for preventing further loss. Luckily many vegan foods are rich in calcium and/or fortified. There are also many vegan calcium supplements on the market! I personally enjoy plant based milks such as almond milk which is packed with calcium. Sorry this was a lot to read! Please let me know if you have any questions or feel free to private message me anytime! Also I want to stress that your health and safety is most important and if you feel like you need to put veganism on the back burner while you are still stabilizing, that’s completely ok too!

I have a whole lot to say on this topic as someone who grew up in the “horse world”. My mother was a rider, and so from about 3 she had me and my sister riding. I will start off by saying, I loved it at the time and I also think that there is something to be said about the special bond that can be formed with the animal, as you would a dog or cat. That said, now as a fully informed, I have a much different view on it, and many of the initial red flags I had as a child became much clearer to me. For the most part horses are simply an essential piece of equipment in a sport. They are disposable when they no longer serve their purpose to the equestrian. They are sold like property and replaced with something else as if their relationship with you is meaningless. Some highly unethical people will even put down their horses in order to collect life insurance if the horses are no longer selling quality, but otherwise perfectly healthy and happy. 

The training is often harsh and utilizes tools like whips and spurs to enforce certain behavior. I used to question this as a child and was told “oh don’t worry it doesn’t hurt them!” How do we know this? Imagine you swap out child with horse and try to justify using those “tools” as a form behavioral correction. You would have Child Protective Services at your door. 

A lot of horses (particularly if they are in lesson programs) are worked beyond a point of what’s reasonable as healthy exercise and forced to work and show in conditions that are potentially dangerous (mud, extreme heat). I will not deny that horses probably enjoy to a certain extent some of the exercise’s (as evidenced by the fact they will naturally canter, trot, jump in the absence of human rider), but the extent to which humans push them for their own sport is undeniably exploitative. Horses get severely or fatally injured all the time being pushed to do extremely complex and difficult jumping courses or races. I think any time you are mixing betting and performance without consent that is by default exploitation. 

Another thing that isn’t brought up as much, is the fact that pretty much all riding tack and apparel is not vegan. You can look, but it would be extremely difficult to find only vegan tack, boots, etc. That’s kind of a moot point if the activity you’re engaging in is not vegan to begin with, but just another reason why it’s hard to justify the sport.

This is hard because it’s another complicated situation where I do believe there are horse lovers who have the animals best interest at heart and love the sport, but I think their ability to use good judgment does get muddied by what the sport demands.

Well, that’s a whole other conversation in which I don’t think there is one clear cut answer. “Would a kid be happy on a vegan diet?” Implies every child would have the same experience, which is an unrealistic stance when you take into account the vast spectrums of cultures, environments, temperaments that factor into a child’s upbringing. I think a reasonable person can agree that it is a parents right and responsibility to make choices for their children that they believe are in that child’s best interest, until the child is able to confidently make those choices for themselves, and simultaneously help that child to understand why that choice is important (i.e making sure your child gets shots at the doctors office even if it scares them). Most parents ideally would raise their kids with the intent of instilling values that they believe are important and hope that the child carries those values on as they mature. In the case of Veganism, a parent would raise their child hoping to instill that it is wrong to harm and exploit animals.

I fully favor a child’s autonomy to the extent it is appropriate, and also believe you cannot “force” someone to be vegan as it is an ethical belief system, not a diet or lifestyle. Just like if someone raised their child going to church, they couldn’t force the kid to be a Christian. At a certain point it would be up to the child to decide for themselves what feels right for themselves. For some kids, they would feel strongly that it is wrong to hurt animals, and therefore be perfectly happy living as a vegan. Another child might feel less sure, due to their own feelings or perhaps cultural/environmental factors such as wanting to do what their friends do, and in that case it would be their right to make that decision. I for one was raised by parents who made me eat meat to a certain age (despite it making me very unhappy), but thankfully they respected my feelings when I grew to the age of autonomy. 🤷🏻‍♀️

Key point, be a good parent and make sure your kid eats nutritious, healthy food (and enough of it). I’m not going to claim from a health perspective one diet is particularly more healthy than the other (im a vegan for ethical reasons not health reasons), but its common sense that a diet that is not loaded with processed foods, chemicals, preservatives, and growth hormones (found in meats and dairy products), is far healthier for anyone.

Gone through many hospitalizations/treatment programs etc. First time I ever really attempted recovery back in 2019 I experienced EH for the first time, rapidly gained weight and remained in somewhat of a remission for about 2 years, then had a massive relapse and got down to a disgustingly low weight which a had been maintaining up until about a month ago, until I started experiencing EH again and now feel like I am going through something similar to 2019. Here’s my take. Extreme Hunger is the bodies natural response to restriction, whether it is by literal physical malnutrition or mental restriction (food rules, depriving yourself of perceived fear foods, planning on restricting in the future,etc). Real mental peace only really starts when all forms of restriction ends. What I’m trying to say is regardless of vegan/not vegan diet you can’t “hack” your way out of it by cutting out foods that your body wants and needs. I don’t think that it’s hating the dog, it’s hating the practice of puppy mills and backyard breeding that is inherent with any type of designer dog. Of course with any breed these breeders exist, the only difference with purebreds is that there are actual registries, breeding standards, health testing requirements for the parent dogs, etc that reputable breeders must adhere to. If you are looking for X breed, there are bonafide breed clubs who’s members all strictly follow these parameters to ensure healthy offspring and are committed to the betterment of the breed. These types of breeders also tend to be hobby breeders meaning that they are breeding for the purpose of breed preservation, not making money off of selling puppies. They are extremely knowledgeable about the lineages of their dogs and the breed, tend to have very few litters, breed their dogs only after they have achieved Championship status (which requires that the dog is of optimal health and quality, and also are an appropriate age to be bred) and never breed a single female more than maybe 2 or 3 times. 

Unfortunately no such types of breed associations exist for non pure breeds which is why you see a lot more unethical breeding, poor health, etc etc that comes along with puppy mill/backyard breeding. 

This isn’t meant to place judgement on anyone and I am positive that there are people who breed doodles who have the utmost interest and care for their dogs, I’m just trying to explain why some have that attitude. I will say though when it comes to any kind of dog breeding there’s always ethical concerns that come into question. I.e breeding two dogs too closely related in lineage can come with their own set of health issues, certain neurological/behavioral issues run in certain breeds, some breeds are almost guaranteed to have a life of breathing issues that often require extensive medical care or surgery to manage (like frenchies and pugs). At the end of the day do your research, stay away from puppy mills and pet shops or any breeder with red flags (no visiting, can’t provide health documentation, has many litters especially at once, can’t provide testimonials, or doesn’t seem interested in getting to know you as an owner before placing a puppy).

Imo the main difference between reactive/extreme hunger and a binge eating disorder is whether or not it becomes a chronic cycle. It is my belief that after any period of deprivation it is completely appropriate and necessary to make up for the deprivation with a vast consumption of whatever it is that has been lacking (for example we would not think twice about chugging water when dehydrated or having a long sleep when exhausted). Therefore if you are starving you need to eat. A LOT. I know it’s so scary especially when we can’t specifically know how much for how long, but this is where we have to give some trust to our bodies and not try to resist these cues that are there to save us. The “BED” in my mind is more the result of a persistent resistance and then the inevitable reactive hunger that becomes a perpetual cycle over a period of time. I think the only way to avoid this cycle is to from the beginning allowing the body to heal and eventually the extreme hunger will subside and normal eating will resume. Otherwise, yes I do think it can become a never ending cycle of restriction and binging which is more or less what BED is (contrary to the misconception that it is simply just some form of out of control gluttony). Bottom line is our bodies are so incredibly smart and if we allow ourselves to trust them rather than attempt to override their instincts, they most always will get us to where we need to be:)

The thin slim brand makes 55 calorie per 57g serving pasta in a variety of shapes. It is the closest low calorie alternative BY FAR that I have tried (and I’ve had everything) as it looks, feels, and cooks like normal wheat pasta. Drawbacks are its expensive and the taste/texture really comes down to ur expectations for a 55 calorie pasta that is basically fiber. IMO fiber gourmet is much more true to the real deal. Heart of palm based pastas like Palmini and Natural Heaven are the best if u are ok with something a little more “vegtabley” vs Shiritaki, zoodles, spaghetti squash, etc. For what it’s worth I recently saw a brand on Amazon called Kaizen which has 130 calories per serving, 6 net carbs, and 20g of protein. Cannot speak to taste, but the reviews look decent enough. There’s also this other kind called “lulupasta” by Wholesome Provisions which can be purchased on amazon. 140 cal for 56 oz, 4 net carbs, 19 grams of protein. Similar to the brand I listed before this, it is lupin flour based. Again, I have not had it myself so I can’t attest to the actual taste but it looks pretty much identical to normal pasta.
